Announced on 17 November, the contract covers the provision of satellite connectivity through Eutelsat’s OneWeb low Earth orbit constellation, alternative positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) capabilities, and technical support. According to US government procurement records , the announcement comes almost five months after the contract was initially awarded in June. The records show that the contract is worth up to $64.46 million, with an initial $6.1 million committed so far. A Space Force procurement justification published in June reveals that the agreement covers a shared pool of OneWeb network capacity to support fixed, land-mobile, and maritime operations. The requirements include up to 1.8 petabytes of shared data, a centralised network management platform, round-the-clock technical support and the ability to activate additional capacity within five days. The document also reveals that the US military has already acquired more than 500 OneWeb terminals. The OneWeb agreement is the second task order issued through the US Space Force Warrior Plans initiative. The first was awarded to SpaceX in May 2026 for Starshield satellite communications services. That contract has a maximum potential value of $511.1 million, including options. In addition to its US Space Force contract, Eutelsat also announced on 17 November that it had secured €600 million in new funding through a bond offering. The company plans to use the funds primarily to repay existing debt due in 2028, replacing it with new borrowing that will not need to be repaid until 2032. This triple system has been called Welopō'ai, which is a portmanteau of two Hawaiian words that means a 'path of family traits', and to understand the mystery behind it requires astronomers to figure out the history of the three objects. A white dwarf is what remains when a star of similar mass to our sun reaches the end of its life. As it begins to run low on hydrogen for nuclear fusion reactions in its core, the star's energy generation begins to falter and its interior starts to contract under gravity . The star's outer layers are shed and they expand out into space, while its core contracts to become an inert white dwarf with a diameter similar to Earth but with a mass generally between half and two-thirds of a solar mass . candidates.title: UK joins 10 other nations in NATO STARLIFT satellite launch initiative
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The UK has joined 10 other countries in a NATO-led initiative to develop a network of flexible satellite launch services, aiming to ensure more reliable access to space and strengthen security.

The UK Ministry of Defence announced on Sunday that the country had signed the NATO STARLIFT initiative alongside Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Türkiye and the Republic of Korea.

STARLIFT aims to work with commercial launch providers and spaceport operators to build a network of launch capabilities across participating countries, making access to space more resilient, responsive and cost-effective.

According to NATO, the initiative will help military users secure launch slots on commercial rockets, including for urgent satellite launches. It will also support improvements to launch infrastructure, logistics and air and maritime traffic management to ensure safe launch operations.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Launch Complex-4E at 7:23 a.m. ET (1223 GMT; 4:23 a.m. local time in California). It was the sixth National Reconnaissance Office launch (NROL) this year to deliver a payload, or group of payloads, to low Earth orbit , all which have been carried out by SpaceX 's workhorse Falcon 9. The launch marks another step in the NRO's effort to expand its intelligence-gathering capabilities through a proliferated network of spacecraft designed to provide more frequent and timely surveillance of locations around the globe. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the NROL-136 mission for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office from California on Nov. 22, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) About two minutes after liftoff, the Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued carrying the classified payloads onward to orbit. The booster then reversed course and returned to Vandenberg, touching down at Landing Zone 4 approximately seven and a half minutes after launch. Saturday's launch was the 14th flight for this particular Falcon 9 booster, dubbed B1097, which previously launched NASA 's Sentinel-6B ocean-monitoring satellite, NROL-172, USSF-259 for the U.S. Space Force , and eight Starlink missions. The network is designed to increase coverage and improve the "capability and resilience" of U.S. intelligence operations in space , according to the NRO's mission website . candidates.raw_excerpt: Doomscrolling might seem like a goofy side effect of our increasingly digitized lives, but some experts are now pegging the phenomenon as a global public health crisis. A major piece of research published in the journal the Lancet Psychiatry estimated that over 10 percent of the world’s population engages in problematic internet use. That phenomenon includes a laundry list of digital behaviors that have become commonplace in the 21st century: compulsive scrolling on social media, of course, but also things like problematic online gambling, compulsive spending, and excessive gaming. These behaviors each share some common characteristics, especially that they’re difficult for the affected person to control. As a result, the problematic internet user experiences consequences around their health, social life, education, work, and overall quality of life. “Digital technologies are now woven into almost every aspect of modern life and bring enormous benefits,” Flinders University professor of mental health and wellbeing Zsolt Demetrovics, who worked on the research, said in a statement . “The challenge is finding ways to reduce harms while preserving the many benefits of being connected.” The issue, the researchers explain, is not with the internet itself — meaning blanket bans or age-related restrictions may only work as stopgaps. Rather, it’s the host of features baked in by companies to keep users hooked and thus generate revenue via ads, clicks, and transactions. These are things like infinite scrolling feeds, targeted recommendations, incessant notifications, and autoplaying short-form videos. Ultimately, the researchers find that responsibility for mitigating this public health concern rests with the companies themselves — though anybody hoping for massive tech corporations like Meta and Google to start regulating themselves is almost certainly setting themself up for major disappointment. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov.22, 1989: NASA launches space shuttle Discovery on classified STS-33 mission for the US military
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night. This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military launched several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites . The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified. NASA's space shuttle Discovery launches on the classified STS-33 mission for the U.S. military on Nov. 22, 1989. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered From its start, the Space Transportation System, better known as the space shuttle, was a compromise between meeting civilian and military needs. NASA saw the vehicle as a means of supporting science research, establishing an on-orbit economy (servicing commercial satellites and flying company payloads) and ultimately, assembling the parts for a space station. The Department of Defense saw the shuttle as an asset to deploying and retrieving reconnaissance satellites, among other projects, some of them classified. It was not until the loss of the space shuttle Challenger, that it was decided that the shuttle would only be used by the military when it was key to national security. Other needs would be met by expendable launch vehicles (ELVs). As an aside, the STS-33 astronauts also spent Thanksgiving in space during this mission. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule. Rømer figured out the pattern and made an accurate prediction for Io's eclipse on Nov. 9, 1676. Then on Nov. 21, he took his findings to the Royal Academy of Sciences and explained that a finite speed of light must be responsible. Danish astronomer Ole Rømer (Image credit: Wikimedia Commons) Why it mattered Understanding that the speed of light is a constant is the key that opened our ability to gauge the scale of the universe, as well as was central to developing modern physics. "The speed of light becomes a sort of ultimate speed limit," Live Science explained in an article about why the speed of light matters. "In fact, objects with mass, be they cars or neutrinos, can't reach the speed of light because they would need infinite energy to do so."

In particular, Feigh points to a phenomenon known as the “verification burden,” a machine learning concept referring to the wasted time humans spend verifying the accuracy of the tech’s work. “At a deeper level, the burden is the cognitive cost of trying to regain authority over work that is partly delegated to a system, while retaining responsibility for the final product,” Feigh explains. candidates.raw_excerpt: Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. The big moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio. The duo launched — along with a power and propulsion element called the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) — aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana in October 2018 , beginning a long and looping trip through the inner solar system. Mercury is a difficult planet to reach because it's so close to the sun . Spacecraft approaching the solar system's innermost planet are accelerated to high velocities by the immense gravitational pull of our star and must shed a great deal of kinetic energy to be captured by Mercury's much weaker tug. So the BepiColombo team designed a trajectory that featured one flyby of Earth , two of Venus and six of Mercury over the course of about seven years. That flight time was increased by a year , however, after the mission suffered an issue with its solar panels, which reduced the power available for the MTM's electric thrusters. BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury will take a total of about six months.
